record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses prior work on a residual-stream refusal direction but tests a different mechanism: attention-head ablation and attention redistribution. It does not measure, remove, add, or otherwise test the difference-in-means direction or the other listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports attention-head ablation and attention-redistribution attack results on refusal behavior. These bear on a related mechanism, not the listed residual-stream direction versions, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. The head maps and SAS values are used to identify attack targets; the discovery sweep compares ARA variants and is not a test of a listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The study ablates attention heads selected by system-prompt attention share (SAS) and runs an attention-redistribution attack (ARA). It never computes, ablates, adds or measures the harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction, so none of V1–V8 is tested. Arditi et al. is discussed only as complementary prior work (Sec. 2, Sec. 6.1). The results concern a different construct: attention routing to system-prompt tokens. They are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also conclude that safety lives in these heads' attention routing, not in their additive residual-stream contribution. On their account, ablation lets the residual stream compensate, while redirection injects a corrupted signal. They call this complementary to Arditi et al.'s removable single direction. Keyword-based refusal classification, the calibration and evaluation prompt overlap, and three confounded architectures limit the claims.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures system-prompt attention by head, then redirects that attention with optimized input tokens or ablates head outputs; it does not use a harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream mean difference or ablate/add that direction.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies across the tested models: Mistral-7B and LLaMA-3-8B have higher reported ARA success than Gemma-2-9B-it. The paper associates this pattern with differences in the concentration of safety attention across layers, but describes the three-model pattern as qualitative.

fits_no_version.finding: Zeroing the output projections of the top-K SAS-ranked heads (K=5 to 20) flips at most 1 of 39/49/50 baseline refusals. Ablating 20 random heads flips none.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In 7–9B instruct models, refusal survives zero-ablation of up to 20 heads that attend most to the system prompt.

fits_no_version.finding: A 5-token ARA attack that minimizes SAS in the top-3 safety layers reaches 36% ASR on Mistral-7B, 30% on LLaMA-3-8B and 1% on Gemma-2-9B over 200 HarmBench prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Redirecting attention away from system-prompt tokens can bypass refusal, with strongly model-dependent success.

record.problems: The study evaluates three 7B–9B models and uses keyword matching to classify refusal or compliance. Its safety-head identification uses the same 200 HarmBench prompts as the main V2 evaluation. The authors note that architecture, tokenizer, alignment procedure, and pretraining data are confounded, and that three architectures do not establish a quantitative relationship between attention distribution and attack success. No general-capability preservation test is reported.
record.rows_left_out: The per-head SAS maps and per-model attention-mass distribution descriptions in Sections 5.1 and Appendix E characterize the attention mechanism and select targets, but do not test a listed residual-stream-direction version. The five-variant discovery sweep in Appendix C/Table 5 is an attack-method comparison rather than a test of the listed direction claim.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction is extracted, ablated or added. No capability check is run. Head ablation is a different intervention.
No weight edit or abliteration of released models.
ARA is a jailbreak, but the study never checks whether it suppresses the refusal direction. No adversarial training against direction ablation.
Residual-stream refusal geometry (single direction, affine set, cone, multiple directions) is not studied.
Harmfulness judgment and the refusal decision are not separated.
No transfer across languages, variants, or base to instruct models.
Training method and timing are not varied. Cross-model differences are confounded with architecture, as the authors note.

record.verdict_notes: The record's links (all rows set to none) and its states are correct. The ARA attack variants are named V1–V5 in the paper; these are not the claim versions. The paper contrasts its results with the original source but makes no measurement on the refusal direction, so no verdict is possible.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means residual-stream direction is found, ablated, or added; general capability is not evaluated.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration based on the residual-stream direction is tested.

ARA redirects attention away from system-prompt positions; the study does not test whether attacks suppress the residual-stream refusal direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
The study does not compare residual-stream refusal geometry as a single direction, affine set, cone, or multiple directions.
Harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are not separately measured.
No cross-language or base-to-instruct transfer of the residual-stream direction is tested.
The study does not vary refusal training method or timing.
